title: Home Is the Place They Leave
author: Mandi Gerth Source: mrsgerthteaches.substack.com
summary: In this personal essay, Mandi Gerth reflects on the grief and gratitude of releasing her firstborn as he completes his senior year, framing the experience through a theology of sacrificial investment in motherhood. She has spent eighteen years operating 'heavy in the red'—pouring out lavishly without counting the cost—trusting that God's economy rewards sacrificial obedience even when the ledger doesn't balance in the short term. The grief she feels now (each familiar moment accompanied by 'this will not happen next year') is not a sign of failure but evidence of fruitfulness: the depth of loss reflects the depth of investment. She argues against the cultural lie that the work of motherhood can be delegated or opted out of without cost, insisting that someone must pay in 'blood, sweat, and tears' to build a home and family. The essay closes with the author's recognition that her obedience has produced people she deeply admires and wants as lifelong friends—a return far exceeding the investment—and that the grief of sending a child out is itself proof that the work mattered.
points: Sacrificial motherhood requires operating 'heavy in the red'—pouring out more than you take in—trusting that God's economy rewards obedience with dividends that only become visible over many years.
The grief of a child leaving is reframed not as loss but as evidence of fruitfulness: you cannot grieve what cost you nothing, so the depth of sorrow reveals the depth of investment.
Each ordinary deposit (boxes of macaroni and cheese, swim lessons, books read over and over) compounds like mustard seeds into 'one hundred fold something so full of glory it takes my breath away.'

The cultural narrative that mothers can outsource the costly work of home-building without consequence is a 'lie'—someone must decide to pay the price, and Gerth argues the return on that payment is immeasurable.
The son the author is releasing is not a loss but the fulfillment of the account: a person she admires deeply and wants as a lifelong friend, which is exactly the payoff she invested toward.
quotes: I wanted to love lavishly and give myself away conspicuously, not counting the sacrifices as pennies I expected to be repaid. Instead, I trusted that God saw the account balance, and he wanted it to be disproportionally weighted toward the five souls who depended upon me.

When I hear my son play the piano, I think to myself: this will not happen next year. When I watch him stand for saxophone solos, I think this will not happen next year. When I talk to him about the books we are reading while he eats trail mix in the kitchen, I think this will not happen next year.

When I examine the nature of my loss and the depth of my sorrow, I find myself humbled. It has never been so clear to me how much all of my labors to grow a person, to nurture a soul and to build a family have born fruit.

It was just boxes and boxes of macaroni and cheese and swim lessons at the YMCA. It was books read over and over and piano lessons paid for. All of those mustard seeds have produced one hundred fold something so full of glory it takes my breath away.
That obedience, which actually came at a great personal cost, has produced the sort of people I want in my life forever, who I admire deeply, and want as lifelong friends.
